Write amplification in flash SSDs escalates as the drive fills primarily due to the fundamental constraint that NAND flash memory can only be erased in large block units, while data is written in much smaller page units. As free space diminishes, the probability that a block contains a mix of valid and invalid data increases, meaning that when the controller needs to reclaim space, it must copy more valid data to new locations before erasing the block. This ratio of actual host writes to physical NAND writes, known as write amplification, grows non-linearly because the controller spends a disproportionate amount of bandwidth moving data that does not need to be moved, effectively degrading performance and increasing wear on the memory cells.

Garbage collection is the background mechanism responsible for this data movement, and its efficiency is directly tied to the block erase granularity. Since the controller cannot erase individual pages, it must identify blocks that are entirely or mostly invalid, copy any remaining valid pages to free blocks, and then erase the source block. In a nearly full drive, finding blocks with low valid data density becomes statistically difficult, forcing the garbage collector to perform more frequent and larger-scale copy operations. This process consumes internal bandwidth that would otherwise be available for host I/O, leading to the latency spikes and throughput drops characteristic of a drive operating near its capacity limit.

Over-provisioning (OP) mitigates this issue by reserving a portion of the physical NAND capacity that is invisible to the host, effectively creating a buffer of always-available free blocks. By maintaining a larger pool of free space than the user sees, the controller can perform garbage collection more efficiently, as it is easier to find blocks with low valid data ratios when there is ample free space to move data into. This headroom allows the drive to absorb write bursts and perform background maintenance without immediately impacting foreground performance, thereby keeping write amplification lower for longer and extending the overall lifespan of the drive by reducing unnecessary erase cycles.

TRIM, or the UNMAP command, addresses write amplification from the host operating system side by informing the SSD which logical blocks are no longer in use. When an application deletes a file, the OS issues a TRIM command, allowing the SSD to mark those corresponding physical pages as invalid immediately rather than waiting for them to be overwritten. This proactive invalidation ensures that when garbage collection eventually runs, it encounters blocks with a higher percentage of invalid data, significantly reducing the amount of valid data that needs to be copied.
